text: King Shaka International Airport (IATA: DUR, ICAO: FALE), abbreviated KSIA, is the primary international airport serving Durban, South Africa, located in La Mercy, KwaZulu-Natal, approximately 35 km (22 mi) north of Durban’s city centre. It opened to passengers on May 1, 2010, 41 days before the start of the 2010 FIFA World Cup, replacing Durban International Airport (ICAO: FADN) and using the same IATA code. The airport was designed by Osmond Lange Architects and Planners and cost R6,800,000,000 (about US$900 million). It was conceptualized due to the limitations of Durban International Airport, which had a 2,400 m (7,874 ft) runway too short for large aircraft like the Boeing 747, leading to reduced international traffic and marginalization compared to Johannesburg and Cape Town. A 2007 study found that upgrading Durban International Airport to full capacity would be 95% more expensive than developing KSIA immediately, and the project faced delays due to disputes between Airports Company South Africa (ACSA) and the Dube TradePort firm, which is backed by the KwaZulu-Natal provincial government, until national transport minister Jeff Radebe intervened in 2004. A tender war between the Illembe and Indiza consortia occurred in 2006, with the Illembe consortium winning the contract after the Indiza group’s appeal was dismissed by the Pietermaritzburg High Court in February 2007. The project’s environmental impact assessment (EIA) was delayed by the South African Department of Environmental Affairs and Tourism but was eventually approved in August 2007 with conditions including the appointment of an environmental control officer, access from the N2 motorway, and mitigation of impacts on a nearby barn swallow colony at Mount Moreland. Construction began on August 24, 2007, and operational testing started in December 2009, with the first commercial flights on May 1, 2010. Despite high construction costs, the terminal was designed without a viewing deck or travellators. The existing Durban International Airport became defunct after KSIA’s completion. British Airways launched a direct service to London Heathrow in October 2018, which was suspended in December 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The airport’s name, "King Shaka International Airport," was approved by the South African Geographical Names Council on January 14, 2010, and became official on February 2, 2010. KSIA is currently building two new heavy-class remote gates, named Foxtrot Aprons, and extending Taxiway Bravo to connect to the runway north of the Taxiway Hotel. The airport precinct is bordered by the M43 road to the north, the Mdloti River to the south, the R102 road to the west, and the N2 freeway to the east. Neighboring communities include Cotton lands, LIV village, oThongathi, Verulam, and eMdloti, with uMhlanga and Ballito further away, generally opposed due to noise concerns. Mount Moreland, 2.6 km south of the airport, is a key roosting site for European barn swallows, and a study found that bird strikes were minimal due to flight patterns occurring before or below the approach path, leading to mitigation measures such as adjusting glide slopes and installing a radar system, which was deployed in January 2009. The passenger terminal, located at the southern end, has a total floor area of 102,000 m² (1,100,000 sq ft) and is capable of handling 7.5 million passengers annually, with arrivals on the lower floor and departures on the upper floor. It features 72 check-in counters, 18 self-service kiosks, 34 aircraft parking bays, and 16 jet bridges, including four that can handle Code F aircraft or four Code C aircraft. The arrivals area has five conveyors and 52 retail outlets across 6,500 m² of retail space. The cargo terminal, located to the north, initially covers 15,000 m² and has a capacity of 150,000 metric tons per year, with potential expansion to 100,000 m² and 1,000,000 metric tons per year. It includes two initial Code F stands, expandable to ten, and is part of the Dube TradePort’s Trade Zone Precinct, which covers 36 hectares and includes logistics, warehousing, and light industry. Shree Property Holdings agreed to build a 60,000 m² facility, and Samsung is to build a TV production plant by the end of 2014 at a cost of $20 million, increasing production from 500,000 to 1 million flat screens. The cargo terminal aims to recapture local air freight traffic from Johannesburg, as KwaZulu-Natal produces about 25,000 metric tons of air cargo annually currently transported by road. The airport operates at sea level, near the Port of Durban, the busiest seaport in the Southern Hemisphere. In the 2024–2025 financial year, KSIA handled 5.04 million passengers, with 4.7 million domestic, 324,919 international, and a small number of unscheduled flights; 40,935 aircraft movements were recorded, mostly domestic. Passenger numbers dropped to 1.5 million in 2020–2021, a 75.4% decrease, with international travel declining by 94.4%. The airport is the third busiest in South Africa, behind OR Tambo International Airport and Cape Town International Airport. It is accessible via the N2 and R102 roads, with the M65 linking them, though it does not extend to the M4, requiring detours. Traffic from the south pays tolls at the La Mercy Ramp Plaza, while traffic from the north pays at the oThongathi Toll Plaza; the R102 offers an untolled alternative. The airport has 6,500 public parking bays and provides shuttle buses and metered taxis. A direct rail line was planned for after 2010, and in 2014, a high-speed monorail was proposed with construction expected in 2017. In late 2024, the eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality announced a feasibility study for a tram-light rail system between the city and the airport, with an exclusive rail link still under consideration.

From the airport, travelers can access the M4 S in uMhlanga, which provides a direct route into the city. The airport features 6,500 public parking bays, distributed between a short-term parkade and a shaded medium-term parking area. Public road transport options include airport shuttle buses and metered taxis, which have been assigned a dedicated pick-up and drop-off zone adjacent to the terminal entrance in the international arrivals area. The main railway line running north from Durban along the North Coast is situated near the R102, and direct rail access was included in the master plans, with construction expected after 2010 as part of the second phase. In 2014, proposals for a new high-speed monorail connecting the city and the airport were introduced, with construction scheduled to begin in 2017. In late 2024, the eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality announced plans for a feasibility study of a tram-light rail system between the Durban city centre and the airport, while an exclusive rail link remained under consideration. However, the tram-light rail feasibility study was cancelled in June 2025 due to the absence of acceptable tenders.
